title: [focus-without-user-activation] Base permission on the initiating document
body: ## Summary Base `focus-without-user-activation` authorization on the document initiating the focus change, rather than the document receiving focus. This separates two questions: whether a document may initiate a focus move, and whether the destination is valid for focusing. Script entry points capture the incumbent global's associated document and pass it explicitly through the dialog and popover algorithms. Declarative invocations use the invoker's document and autofocus uses the element's document. Related: whatwg/html#12032, whatwg/html#12470, and whatwg/html#11839. ## Motivation An allowed parent should be able to delegate focus into a child with the feature denied. Conversely, a restricted initiator should not be authorized just because its target has the feature enabled, has transient activation, or already has focus. Once an embedded application receives focus, it also needs to manage its controls, delegate to nested content, and reclaim focus from that content. These are the compatibility cases described in whatwg/html#11839. The [TPAC 2024 resolution](https://github.com/w3c/webappsec-permissions-policy/issues/273#issuecomment-2384287101) requires parent to child delegation. ## Allow focus steps ```text allow focus steps(focusSetterDocument): 1. If focusSetterDocument is not fully active, return false. 2. If focusSetterDocument is allowed to use focus-without-user-activation policy, return true. 3. If focusSetterDocument's relevant global has transient activation, return true. 4. Return has focus steps(focusSetterDocument). ``` The target's policy and activation no longer grant permission. `has focus steps` includes focus in descendant navigables and requires the top-level traversable to have system focus. A restricted document can therefore manage focus while it or one of its descendants has focus. ## Intended behavior Let allowed document A contain restricted B and D, with restricted C nested inside B. Unless noted, there is no transient activation. | Scenario | Result | |---|---| | A focuses an element in restricted B | Allow: A's policy authorizes it | | Focused B focuses another element in B | Allow | | Focused B delegates to child C | Allow | | C is focused; B retakes focus into its own document | Allow | | Focused B hands focus to sibling D or back to A | Allow | | Focus has moved to D; B tries to reclaim it without activation | Deny | | Unfocused B targets allowed A | Deny: A's policy does not authorize B | | Only D has activation; B tries to focus D | Deny: D's activation does not authorize B | | Unfocused D targets B while focus is in B's child C | Deny | | B has transient activation and requests focus outside its subtree | Allow | An allowed or already focused initiator may request focus across an opener/popup relationship, subject to existing access and focusing rules, this does not override restrictions on system level window focus. A restricted popup with neither transient activation nor focus in its subtree fails the permission check even if its opener has the feature enabled. *** /acknowledgements.html ( diff ) /form-elements.html ( diff ) /interaction.html ( diff ) /interactive-elements.html ( diff ) /popover.html ( diff )
